strengths: Addresses an important and difficult problem: environment-scale, multi-room 3D scene generation from text, where purely 2D/video-based generative priors struggle with long-range and cross-room consistency.
The geometry-first decoupling is sensible: an explicit mesh scaffold provides a strong structural anchor, and the paper clearly separates global layout from local appearance synthesis.

The mesh-conditioned image synthesis design conditions on depth, progressively accumulated wall textures, and reconstructed object meshes; the ablation study gives useful evidence for the importance of each conditioning component.

Several technical components are reasonable and well-motivated: rotational-similarity view ordering, projective texture accumulation with occlusion/back-face filtering, depth-edge validation, and geometry-regularized 3DGS optimization.
Qualitative results show diverse, high-fidelity multi-room scenes with plausible transitions and object-level coherence; the user study suggests a clear preference over several existing baselines.
The manuscript is generally clear, well-structured, and includes limitations for single-story layouts and incomplete object back faces.
weaknesses: The method is not actually text-only as claimed: the appendix states that SAM3 requires user-provided positive/negative point prompts for object segmentation. This manual, per-object, per-room annotation contradicts the central 'from an input text prompt' claim and directly undermines the scalability argument. The suggested VLM automation is not implemented or evaluated.

Reproducibility is limited: the pipeline relies on proprietary or future models (Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, SAM-3D-Objects) and on undisclosed details such as layout-generation prompts/validation rules, image-verification threshold, Canny parameters, and texture-projection filters. No code, model weights, or detailed reproduction protocol are provided.

The evaluation does not adequately support the multi-room/scalability claims. Baselines are largely single-room methods, and the qualitative comparison focuses on one room within a generated environment. There are no quantitative metrics for layout adherence, cross-room consistency, object placement accuracy, connectivity, or scaling behavior with the number of rooms.

The claim that the approach is the 'first' scalable multi-room text-to-3D method and the claims of 'arbitrarily-sized' scenes are not demonstrated. The results show only a handful of generated layouts, with no runtime, memory, or room-count scaling analysis, despite the single NVIDIA RTX A5000 setup.

The perceptual study lacks important details: participant selection, randomization, confidence intervals/error bars, number of evaluated scenes, and statistical significance. The 96.2% average pairwise preference, including 100% against some baselines, is very high and may reflect a ceiling effect or unfair comparison conditions.

Baseline comparisons appear potentially unfair or mismatched: SpatialGen is given our generated layout, object locations, and reference image, while several other baselines receive only text prompts or a single image. None are adapted for true multi-room generation, so the comparison does not establish superiority in the multi-room setting claimed as the main contribution.

The depth-edge verification only measures missing mesh edges (false negatives) and does not penalize hallucinated extra structural elements. The pass/fail threshold is unspecified, and the verification is not itself quantitatively evaluated.

The ablation is limited to conditioning-image variants on a single six-room layout and theme. It does not ablate the LLM layout generation, manual object segmentation, SAM-3D-Objects reconstruction, depth regularization, view-selection strategy, verification loop, or number of generated views.

Object placement and physical plausibility are not quantitatively evaluated. The method relies on SAM-3D-Objects for reconstructed geometry and poses, which can be incomplete or inaccurate, and manual segmentation may artificially improve consistency in the reported results.

The final appearance depends heavily on a proprietary image model (Nano Banana Pro) and on iterative projections that can accumulate seams, blur, and degradation. These failure modes are acknowledged only qualitatively and are not analyzed experimentally.

strengths: Addresses an important and ambitious problem: environment-scale, multi-room 3D scene generation from text, with potential impact for VR, games, and interior design.
The geometry-first decomposition into a mesh scaffold for global structure and image synthesis for local appearance is sensible and well motivated for improving multi-view consistency.

The pipeline is technically detailed, combining LLM-based floor-plan generation, mesh construction, object instantiation, projective wall texturing, mesh-conditioned image synthesis, depth-edge validation, and 3DGS optimization.
The ablation study supports the claimed benefit of the full mesh conditioning, showing gains over depth-only, depth+objects, and depth+walls+bboxes variants.
Qualitative results are visually compelling and demonstrate diverse themes and some multi-room scenes, with comparisons suggesting better object and structural consistency than several baselines.
The user study evaluates overall quality, object consistency, and structural consistency across 31 participants, which is more than a purely automatic 2D-metric evaluation.
The paper is generally clearly written and the main pipeline stages are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The method is not actually text-only despite the central claim: the appendix states that SAM3 is used in interactive point-based mode, requiring a user to provide positive and negative point prompts per object/view. This manual annotation step severely undermines the claimed automatic text-to-multi-room generation and scalability.

The paper relies heavily on proprietary or closed-source models and APIs (Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, SAM-3D-Objects, Depth Pro), with no released code or sufficient reproduction details. This makes independent verification and reproducibility difficult.

The key multi-room contribution is not quantitatively evaluated. The automatic metrics are only 2D image-quality/aesthetic scores, and there is no standard 3D metric for multi-room consistency, layout adherence, cross-room connectivity, or scalability.

Baselines are mostly single-room methods and are adapted with different levels and types of input. Some receive text prompts, some receive a generated image, and SpatialGen receives our generated layout, object locations, and reference image. This makes the quantitative comparison difficult to interpret as a fair test of the paper's multi-room claims.

The perceptual study is weakly reported: no confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, number of scenes evaluated, participant demographics, or inter-rater reliability. The near-perfect preference rates, including 100% against some baselines, are suspicious without stronger study details.

Important implementation details are missing: the depth-edge validation threshold is not specified, regeneration/failure rates are not reported, floor-plan sampling and validity rules are only vaguely described, runtime/compute/memory statistics are absent, and object segmentation/placement details are largely deferred to the appendix.

The scientific novelty is limited: the work is largely an engineering pipeline combining existing components (LLM layout generation, SAM3 segmentation, SAM-3D-Objects reconstruction, image diffusion, projective texturing, and 3DGS). It does not introduce a fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical insight.
The reported ablation is conducted on only one six-room gothic mansion layout and one trajectory, so the generality of the ablation conclusions is unclear.

The layout and object-placement stages are not evaluated directly. There is no metric for floor-plan correctness, object placement plausibility, object counts, collision rates, or whether generated rooms match the text prompt.

The final 3DGS optimization uses only soft depth regularization to the mesh scaffold, not a hard geometric constraint. There is no quantitative analysis of geometric drift or depth fidelity in the final representation.

The camera generation strategy assumes eye-level/perimeter/overhead cameras and rectangular or simple room layouts. It is unclear how the method handles non-rectangular rooms, complex openings, or larger buildings.

The object reconstruction from SAM-3D-Objects is acknowledged to produce incomplete back faces and coarse textures, but the paper does not address how this affects final scene quality or multi-view consistency.

The claim that the approach scales linearly with the number of rooms is unsupported by runtime or resource measurements, and manual segmentation/annotation would likely make the pipeline scale unfavorably with object count.
The paper omits discussion of societal impacts, potential misuse of generated 3D environments, and data attribution/licensing issues for the proprietary generative models used.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: environment-scale, multi-room text-to-3D scene synthesis with navigable outputs.

The geometry-first decomposition into a mesh scaffold and mesh-conditioned appearance synthesis is intuitive and empirically effective; the scaffold provides a useful 3D anchor for both global and local consistency.
The pipeline combines existing components in a sensible way, and the resulting qualitative results across diverse themes and layouts are impressive.
The paper compares against many baselines and includes automatic metrics, a 31-participant perceptual study, and component ablations.
The ablation study supports the importance of textured walls, reconstructed objects, and depth conditioning.
Limitations such as single-story restriction and incomplete object backfaces are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The work does not explicitly declare a contribution type; under the default Algorithms/General assessment, its technical novelty is limited, as it mainly integrates existing tools (LLM floorplan, Flux/Nano Banana, SAM3, SAM-3D-Objects, Depth Pro, 3DGS). It is better viewed as Applied/Systems, but then reproducibility and system-level validation become more critical.

Reproducibility is a major concern: the method relies on several proprietary or future-generation models/APIs (Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, SAM-3D-Objects) and does not provide code, prompts, seeds, thresholds, or enough implementation detail for independent replication.

The pipeline is not fully automatic in the reported results: the appendix describes interactive point-based SAM3 segmentation with human positive/negative prompts. The automated alternative is only mentioned, not evaluated, undermining the 'from text prompt' and scalability claims.

Quantitative evaluation lacks direct 3D consistency and geometry metrics (e.g., multi-view reprojection error, depth accuracy, Chamfer/F-score). CLIP-IQA and CLIP Aesthetic are 2D metrics, and the user study is subjective, so the central 3D-consistency claim is not rigorously measured.

Baseline comparisons appear potentially unfair: most baselines target single rooms and are evaluated on our close-up trajectories or supplied with our generated layout/image. The near-100% preference rate may reflect baseline setup rather than a fully controlled comparison.

Several key details are unspecified, including the image-verification recall threshold, regeneration rate, layout validation rules, object-placement heuristics, and runtime/cost. The claimed linear scaling with number of rooms is not empirically quantified.

Ablations are conducted on only one layout/theme and one trajectory, with no error bars or significance tests. The user study also lacks statistical testing and information about blinding/randomization.

The final appearance quality depends heavily on the proprietary Nano Banana Pro model, but there is no controlled study of how much of the result is attributable to the mesh conditioning versus the external image generator.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult problem: environment-scale, multi-room, navigable 3D scene generation from text, with a clear geometry-first decomposition that separates scene structure from local appearance.

Proposes a coherent and technically plausible pipeline: LLM-generated floor plans, mesh scaffold construction, image-based object instantiation, projective wall texturing, iterative mesh-conditioned view synthesis, and geometry-regularized 3DGS optimization.

The explicit mesh scaffold provides a useful geometric anchor for multi-view and cross-room consistency, and qualitative results show diverse, plausible multi-room outputs including close-up and transitional views.
Ablations support the importance of the full mesh-conditioning signal (depth, textured walls, reconstructed objects) and of mesh-based 3DGS initialization and depth regularization for 3D consistency.

A perceptual study with 31 participants reports large improvements over baselines in object consistency, structure consistency, and overall quality, with high pairwise preference for the proposed method.
The appendix and main paper provide useful implementation details, prompts, baseline adaptation details, per-scene scaling statistics, layout-LLM statistics, and a navigability analysis.
The pipeline is claimed to be backbone-agnostic and includes a fully local path with Flux2-Klein-9B, partially mitigating dependence on proprietary image generation APIs.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with informative figures, qualitative comparisons, and ablation tables.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on proprietary or closed-source foundation models (Claude Opus, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3/SAM-3D-Objects, Depth Pro) and interactive point-prompt segmentation raises reproducibility, cost, and scalability concerns; no accessible code/data link is evident in the manuscript.

Limited algorithmic novelty: the method largely integrates existing components rather than introducing a new generative model or conditioning architecture; mesh-conditioned synthesis is implemented by prompting an off-the-shelf image model with rendered mesh and reference imagery, which is related to prior layout-guided 3D scene generation.

Evaluation is not fully convincing: the user study has only 31 participants and lacks statistical tests, demographic details, and variance estimates; near-saturated pairwise preferences (93-100%) may partly reflect weak baseline adaptations rather than robust gains. Baselines are adapted with different inputs, e.g., SpatialGen is provided our layout and initial object image, which could bias comparisons.

Automatic metrics (CLIP-IQA+, CLIP Aesthetic) are 2D image-quality measures and do not directly assess 3D consistency; 3D metrics are reported on separate, small evaluation sets, and the perceptual ablation is conducted on only a single scene.

Several claims appear overstated: 'first approach' for scalable multi-room 3D synthesis and 'scales linearly' need broader comparison and more formal scaling analysis; the scaling table is difficult to interpret and does not fully substantiate linearity across all components.

The method is limited to single-story scenes and depends on SAM-3D-Objects, which can leave incomplete back faces or missing detail in occluded regions; object placement may still produce intersections, floating objects, or unrealistic layouts, and these failure modes are not quantitatively evaluated.

The depth-edge recall validation uses an unspecified threshold and only penalizes missing structural edges while allowing extra hallucinated objects, so its reliability and effect on final quality are not fully established beyond a limited ablation.

There is no societal-impact or ethical discussion, such as potential biases inherited from LLMs/image models, misuse of generated environments, or copyright/licensing issues for generated assets, and the limitations discussion is brief.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult problem: environment-scale, multi-room 3D scene generation from text, with an explicit goal of maintaining both local object consistency and global multi-room coherence.

The geometry-first decoupling into a mesh scaffold and mesh-conditioned appearance synthesis is a sensible systems design. Using explicit structure to anchor image synthesis is well motivated and appears to improve consistency in the qualitative results.

The overall pipeline is substantial and integrates several modern components (LLM layout generation, depth-conditioned image synthesis, object reconstruction, projective texturing, 3DGS optimization) into a working multi-room scene generator.

Qualitative results are diverse and visually strong, showing multi-room layouts, close-up object views, and various themes. The supplementary scaling table suggests the system can be run on scenes with up to 12 rooms.

The user study, while limited, and the ablation study provide some evidence that mesh conditioning and mesh-regularized 3DGS improve consistency over baselines. The ablations isolating depth, wall texture, object reconstruction, and 3DGS depth loss are useful.
The method handles a setting that most prior image/video-based scene generators do not: coherent multi-room synthesis. If made fully reproducible and automatic, this direction would be impactful.
weaknesses: The method is not truly text-only or automatic as claimed. Object segmentation uses SAM3 in an interactive point-prompted mode, requiring human annotation for objects in generated images. The appendix only states this could be automated by a VLM, but no automated version is evaluated. This manual step directly undermines the claims of scalability, 'from a text prompt', and linear scaling with rooms.

The pipeline depends heavily on proprietary or unavailable foundation models and APIs, including Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects. The manuscript advertises 'Code & data' but no visible link or release details are provided. Reproducibility is therefore very weak: key results cannot be verified without access to the same closed models and exact prompts/settings.

Technical novelty is incremental. The work largely combines existing components: LLM-generated floor plans, depth-conditioned image-to-image synthesis, projective texture accumulation, SAM-based segmentation, single-image object reconstruction, and depth-regularized 3DGS. The 'mesh-conditioned diffusion' contribution is implemented mainly as prompt-based image editing with a rendered mesh and style reference, not as a principled conditional diffusion model or ControlNet-style mechanism.

The claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'first scalable multi-room 3D synthesis from text', 'arbitrarily-sized 3D scenes', and 'robust 3D consistency' are not adequately supported. There is no multi-room baseline comparison, no evaluation of layout correctness, object placement plausibility, or cross-room consistency across long trajectories, and no quantification of manual annotation cost.

The evaluation has fairness and validity concerns. Baselines are mostly single-room/specialized methods, and some are evaluated on close-up object-rotation trajectories outside their intended design. SpatialGen is given this method's generated layout, object locations, and reference image, while 100% preference over it is reported, which is implausibly high without stronger controls or statistics. The user study uses only 31 participants, one scene for the perceptual ablation, and reports no confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-rater reliability.

Automatic metrics are insufficient for the central claim of 3D consistency. CLIP-IQA+ and CLIP aesthetic scores measure 2D image quality, not 3D structure or multi-view consistency. The proposed reprojection and mesh-alignment metrics are not clearly defined or shown to be reliable across methods, and the paper itself notes that the 2D metrics do not capture 3D consistency.

Important implementation details are missing or unclear. The edge-recall validation threshold is never specified. The depth normalization and comparison between predicted depth and rendered mesh depth are not fully described. Definitions of M-MAE, M-RMSE, N-Cos, and N-Ang are incomplete. Table A3 has garbled/unlabeled columns and units, making the scaling and cost analysis difficult to interpret.

The method has unresolved failure modes that are acknowledged but not analyzed: SAM-3D-Objects often produces incomplete back faces, single-view object reconstruction may yield coarse object textures, projective texturing can create seams, and depth regularization against the mesh may conflict with newly hallucinated objects that are absent from the scaffold. Object placement/collision handling is heuristic and not quantitatively evaluated.

Clarity and presentation need substantial work. Section numbering is inconsistent (e.g., '3.1.2' appears under Section 3.2), several table labels and metrics are undefined or malformed, and the manuscript contains multiple typos and unclear captions. This makes the technical claims harder to verify.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult problem: environment-scale, multi-room text-to-3D scene generation with navigable 3D outputs.
The geometry-first decoupling into a mesh scaffold and conditioned appearance synthesis is sensible and is supported by qualitative results across diverse themes and room layouts.

The pipeline is technically detailed, including LLM-based floor-plan generation, scaffold construction, object instantiation with SAM3 and SAM-3D-Objects, progressive wall-texture accumulation, iterative mesh-conditioned image synthesis, and geometry-regularized 3DGS optimization.
Ablations are informative and isolate the contributions of object reconstruction, textured walls, edge-recall validation, mesh-based 3DGS initialization, and mesh depth regularization.
The perceptual study and quantitative comparisons suggest clear improvements in multi-view/object consistency and visual quality over several image-, panorama-, and video-based baselines.
The paper includes useful scalability, cost, and navigability analyses, and it acknowledges limitations such as single-story layouts and incomplete object back faces.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited by heavy reliance on proprietary or external foundation models, including Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro API, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects; the fully local alternative is mentioned but not evaluated in comparable detail.

The object segmentation stage uses interactive point prompts in the main pipeline, which weakens the claim of fully automatic text-to-3D generation and raises questions about user effort and reproducibility.

The baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: many baselines are single-room methods evaluated on one generated room, and some are given our layout or reference images while others receive only text prompts.

The evaluation lacks ground-truth 3D scenes and direct geometry metrics for most baselines; mesh-alignment metrics are only applicable to the proposed method, and the cross-view depth reprojection metric is a proxy rather than a complete measure of 3D consistency.

The user study uses 31 participants and reports very high preference rates without confidence intervals or detailed protocol controls, so the strength of the perceptual conclusion should be interpreted cautiously.
The layout generation assumes relatively simple rectangular rooms and single-story layouts; robustness to complex, non-Manhattan, or multi-floor environments is not demonstrated.
The edge-recall validation measures missing structural edges but not extra hallucinated structural geometry, so it only partially enforces geometric fidelity.

The technical novelty is largely system-level integration of existing components such as LLM layout generation, depth-conditioned image synthesis, SAM-based object reconstruction, and 3DGS; the algorithmic advance over prior mesh- or layout-conditioned pipelines may be incremental.
